metadata.document_title: Emergency Clinical Protocol: Acute Coronary Syndrome, Myocardial Infarction Red Flags, and Pre-Hospital Interventions

sections.section_title: Acute Coronary Syndrome Presentation and Red Flags
sections.text: Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) encompasses non-ST-segment elevation acute coronary syndromes (unstable angina and NSTEMI) and ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Classic red-flag symptoms include severe, crushing, squeezing, or heavy substernal chest pain or pressure lasting more than 15 minutes that is not fully relieved by rest. The pain frequently radiates to the left arm, both arms, neck, jaw, throat, back, or epigastrium. Associated emergency symptoms include profuse cold diaphoresis (sweating), acute shortness of breath (dyspnea), nausea, vomiting, dizziness, lightheadedness, and profound fatigue. Atypical presentations without overt chest pain ('silent ischemia') occur frequently in elderly patients, women, and individuals with long-standing diabetes.

sections.section_title: Immediate Pre-Hospital and Emergency Department Actions
sections.text: Upon recognition of acute coronary syndrome red flags, immediate emergency medical services (999/911/108) must be dispatched without delay. Emergency pre-hospital actions include: 1. Aspirin: Administer chewable Aspirin 300 mg (or 162-325 mg non-enteric coated) immediately, chewed for rapid buccal absorption and platelet cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) inhibition, unless confirmed anaphylactic allergy exists; 2. Sublingual Nitroglycerin (Glyceryl Trinitrate / GTN): Administer 1 spray or 0.4 mg tablet sublingually every 5 minutes (up to a maximum of 3 doses) for persistent ischemic chest pain, provided systolic blood pressure is >= 90 mmHg; 3. Supplemental Oxygen: Administer supplemental oxygen ONLY if oxygen saturation (SpO2) is below 90%, as hyperoxia induces coronary vasoconstriction and increases reperfusion injury.

Nitroglycerin (GTN) administration is strictly contraindicated in the following acute clinical situations: 1. Hypotension: Systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg (or a drop >= 30 mmHg below baseline); 2. Severe bradycardia (heart rate < 50 beats per minute) or severe tachycardia (heart rate > 100 bpm in the absence of heart failure); 3. Phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE-5) inhibitor usage: Nitroglycerin must NOT be given if the patient has taken Sildenafil or Vardenafil within the previous 24 hours, or Tadalafil within the previous 48 hours, due to catastrophic, refractory, life-threatening profound systemic hypotension and cardiovascular collapse; 4. Suspected right ventricular infarction (frequently associated with inferior STEMI): marked preload dependency leads to profound hemodynamic shock upon nitrate-mediated venodilation.

sections.section_title: Definitive Reperfusion Therapy and Time Windows
sections.text: For confirmed STEMI, emergency reperfusion therapy is paramount to salvage myocardium. Primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with cardiac catheterization and stent placement is the preferred treatment if it can be achieved within 120 minutes of STEMI diagnosis (door-to-balloon time < 90 minutes in PCI-capable centers). If timely PCI is unavailable within 120 minutes, intravenous fibrinolytic therapy (e.g., Alteplase, Tenecteplase) should be administered within 30 minutes of emergency arrival ('door-to-needle' time < 30 min) in the absence of absolute contraindications such as prior hemorrhagic stroke or active internal bleeding.
